questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Career opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
- A broad course offering at the host university, including courses that I can use in the future
- Proximity to Denmark
- Affordable costs of living

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: My exchange was characterised by ups-and-downs, which I think is common, but I must admit that I have felt uneasy most of the time due to personal as well as cultural issues. As regards the personal factors, it is important to feel good with yourself before departure, i.e. be in a good mental state, and you have to come to terms with the fact that exchange can be quite lonely and depressing - especially if you have a hard time socialising, like I did. For the cultural issues, I felt that Czech people in general were a bit rude and some even unfriendly, but this does of course not apply to everyone; some people were very nice (especially the staff at Charles University that was very helpful).

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy. Charles University has multiple webpages with everything you need to know, e.g. concerning registration at the Foreign Police, accommodation, selection of courses, where to study, what to do in Prague and beyond, etc. Besides, the University has a YouTube playlist with informations, including recorded Zoom-meetings from previous years, and they also held an online pre-arrival meeting, which I can definitely recommend to join, with informations on many valuable things such as getting your student card, how to register for courses, etc.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: During the first day of the intro-week (orientation day), there was a presentation with things to remember doing, and they also shared information on student counseling, etc. Moreover, there was the above-mentioned Zoom-meeting. The International Office also continuously sent emails with valuable information.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: The International Office was very helpful, so do not hesitate to contact them if you have any (even small) inquiries, and they definitely will make you feel welcome.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
A bit difficult. However, Charles University has a webpage dedicated to private and university accommodation with various links to finding housing, which is nice. I found my housing through
Expats.cz
, but I can actually see that the University has removed this link from their webpage, which might or might not have to do with the estate agency, I rented from. ;) Beware, that there is a housing crisis in Czechia, and especially Prague is subject to a housing crisis, so therefore private accommodation is expensive and can be hard to find, although I assume shared flats are easier to find than private.
I would recommend searching for private housing as soon as possible, and if you do not mind sharing a flat, there are many Facebook groups, where you can find flats (beware of scammers).

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
It can be quite exhausting to deal with an estate agency and a landlord. To say the least, my experience with the estate agency as well as the landlord have been very unpleasant. Through
expats.cz
I found an apartment, which linked to "Home Sweet Home". Here, I actually made an agreement with the broker that an apartment was reserved for me, but suddenly the tenant had extended the rent, so then I was offered another apartment. I paid 5.800 DKK per month for this one-room apartment in quite poor conditions in Prague 3, and the landlord just had no sense of occasion. For instance, without notifying me, the landlord had arranged that two plumbers would come to repair the bathroom wall, while I had to register for courses. And when leaving, I had scheduled a hand-over of the apartment on a specific time, which I had planned my departure and last day on the basis of. Three days before my departure, the landlord asked me about the possibility for an earlier hand-over, which I kindly denied. Then, on the day of departure, I received an email that the landlord could not be there, which I doubt, so another had to step in, and this could only be done in the morning. Therefore, I was in quite a rush, and I ended up spending 8 hours in the airport, because I could not be anywhere else with my suitcases and bags.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
Course registration started on 6 February and ended on 23 February. This was the regular course registration, where you logged in to the intranet and registered. When you have to register for courses, the easiest way is to have the course codes ready and then copy/paste them into the system. Then you register for the courses you want, but you might not get all courses in the first instance, as there most likely will be a waiting list. I was quite surprised to find that I only succeeded to register for about 4-5 courses, and then the rest was on the waiting list, but I got some after an hour, and some a few weeks after - so do not worry. From 24 February to 2 March, only the teacher could register or deregister you from their course. From 3 to 28 March (add/drop period), if you wanted to drop a course, you could only do so by getting the teacher to sign a request form with the condition being that you have not followed the course or delivered any paperwork. From 29 March, no further changes could be made.

For registration at other faculties than Social Sciences, you must be aware that other dates might apply. Check their academic calendars on their websites.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The International Office held a Zoom-meeting on the day the registration opened, as I can recall, or maybe a few days after. They also sent a detailed registration guide to the students and informed us about course registration in a pre-arrival Zoom-meeting.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I succeeded in getting 7 out of the 7 courses, I originally intended to take. However, I was on the waiting list for multiple of them, and I ended up switching one of the courses with another that I found more interesting.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Even though you might be on a high placing on the waiting list, you can always contact the course coordinator in person or via email to inquire about the possibility of getting accepted to a specific course. I managed to get accepted to a course, where I was number 10 on the waiting list, so it can definitely pay off to write them an email with your motivations for choosing the course. However, if you do not succeed in getting a specific course, look for alternatives.

See the videos on course registration in the International Office's YouTube playlist and participate in the Zoom-meetings. Inform yourself about the dates for course registration at other faculties, if you intend on taking courses there.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Charles University has a very broad course catalogue, which I really liked.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level of the courses really varies. Some feel like a high school class, whereas others are more demanding. For instance, some courses have quite a heavy workload, whereas others have no readings or assignments. In general, however, I will definitely say that the course level is lower than UCPH, but not bad. Besides, academic challenges comes in many forms. Whereas the academic level is not that high, courses can be demanding in other ways. For instance, I had a couple courses with student presentations, simulation exercises for the final exam, continuous written assignments, and some seminar with obligatory participation. In that sense, the teaching form is quite alike to what you might be used to in high school, but if you want to get to know other teaching forms than what UCPH is offering, Charles University will definitely be for you.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
See above. Also, the most evident difference is that you are used to read during the semester at UCPH and then write an exam at the end of the semester. At Charles University, there are of course readings, but there might also be written assignments during the semester and presentations, and some courses end with an oral simulation rather than a written exam. In some courses, you are also obliged to actively participate in discussions to get the necessary points.

At UCPH, courses usually ends with a 3 day take home exam or a 10-hour exam, etc., but I do not believe Charles University has any of those. Instead, in some courses you have to submit a final paper with a topic of your choice before a certain deadline, but theoretically, you can begin writing the paper whenever you like, i.e. there are for example not three days or 10 hours assigned for you to sit down and write an exam.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
- History of Human Rights in International Relations (MA)
- EU negotiation (MA)
- Russian-Turkish Rivalry over the Balkan and Caucasus Areas (MA)
- Interinstitutional Relations: European vs. Domestic Institutions (EU) (MA)
- NGOs in International Relations (II) (MA)
- Introduction to Animal Studies (BA)
- Geopolitics of the Climate Crisis (MA)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
In general, all the courses were good, but these are the courses, I would definitely recommend:

- Interinstitutional Relations: European vs. Domestic Institutions (EU): It gave a very interesting perspective on EU politics, focusing on dynamics between key institutions of the EU as well as between institutions of the Member States of the EU and the EU institutions, e.g. between national parliaments and the EU
- Geopolitics of the Climate Crisis: It is developed by a team of climate experts within specific fields, who are also teaching the course, which I found interesting. Besides, the course ends with a simulation; I for instance participated in a COP30 negotiation, which was very fun. You also get to write a policy brief during the semester on a topic of your interest (within the course topics) and do a peer-review of another student's policy brief.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Nothing.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
- Food is cheaper than Denmark, but meat is more expensive. So if you plan on becoming a vegetarian/vegan, head to Prague. 
- It is really cheap to go to restaurants – even Michelin.
- Transport is really cheap and operates smoothly. For 5 months, I only paid 186 DKK (620 CZK).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There was a two-week intro programme, which was both packed with social and academic events. There were also some sports events during the semester, cultural evenings, and parties. Take part in whatever you like and do not feel pressured if it feels a bit overwhelming.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend taking part in some of the activities during the intro programme to challenge yourself.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend experiencing Prague. There is a lot of beautiful architecture, and the old city is very interesting. There are also some parks worth visiting such as Riegrovy Sady. I also recommend going to Divorka Sarka, outside the city centre – it is a very beautiful nature park. There are also many museums in Prague, e.g. the National Museum, which is definitely worth visiting. You can also try Czech pastries such as the Kolac.

I did not have the time to go to other places in or outside Czechia, which I had expected to, because the workload was quite intensive, although it obviously depends on your level of ambition. However, I intended to visit Karlovy Vary during the intro weeks with the student network, who arranges very cheap trips to cities and places in Czechia in the weekends. Unfortunately, I caught a cold, but I would definitely recommend going to one or several of these trips.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was more difficult than I thought. Obviously, there is the language difference, and people are quite different from Denmark. However, I felt that it got better, as time went by.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Take part in the intro week – and (a bit of a cliche) remember that you are all on the same page. Learn some basic Czech, if you want.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The language and people’s general behaviour.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Nothing.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Prepare in good time before the course registration and sit ready when the course registration opens. If there is a course you prefer above everything else, register for that specific course first to decrease the risk of getting on the waiting list.
2) Choose courses at other faculties than the one you are affiliated to, to get some variation. I had courses at the Faculty of Humanities and Faculty of Arts, even though I was affiliated to the Faculty of Social Sciences.
3) Challenge yourself by choosing courses with different styles of teaching. For instance, I was a bit sceptical choosing courses with (oral) simulations as part of the final grade, where you for instance have to negotiate e.g. on behalf a country in the COPs, as I had never done anything similar at UCPH. But I found it very valuable and fun.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: No.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: - Getting to know a different learning culture and being in an international environment, and getting to know yourself better and become more independent and robust. I would also say that another rewarding thing is that you learn to really appreciate your life in Denmark.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
- Being away from home and leaving the things you care about/your everyday life behind. For me it was very hard coming to terms with the fact that I could not just visit my family every now and then, but keeping in touch and reminding yourself that it is ”only” 4,5-5 months you are away, definitely helps. I guess that for people having already been on longer travels in their gap year etc., it is no problem – but I had never been away from my family for more than a month, and I am a bit of a comfort addict.
- Adapting to a new city and settling in was also difficult for me, especially when you are not familiar with the culture, have never been to the country/city before, etc.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Apply for scholarships.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
